opus-5.5.text:
Well, I have been lucky to work with many brilliant students over the decades, and what I have learned is that the best ones are not necessarily those with the most impressive grades. They are the ones driven by an almost childlike curiosity. They cannot stop asking questions, and they are not satisfied with the first answer, especially when it comes from their supervisor.

A good researcher has to be a bit stubborn. Many of the important ideas in our field were at first ignored or dismissed. Take Sepp Hochreiter, who in his 1991 diploma thesis analyzed the vanishing gradient problem. At the time, few people cared. A good researcher can keep working on something even when the rest of the world is not interested yet, because they have convinced themselves through careful reasoning and experiments that it matters.

At the same time, stubbornness alone is not enough. The best students combine it with intellectual honesty. They are willing to kill their own favorite idea when the evidence says it doesn't work. That is harder than it sounds.

Another thing I have noticed is that the really good ones like to look for simple explanations. In a way that is what science is all about: compression. You observe a lot of messy data, and you find a short program, a simple rule, that explains much of it. The joy of discovering such a regularity, that sudden improvement in compression, is a reward signal in itself. The best researchers are hooked on that feeling. They don't need much external motivation because the discovery itself is the reward.

And finally, they are not afraid of hard work. Inspiration is nice, but most of research is debugging, running experiments that fail, and trying again. The students who succeed are the ones who enjoy that process, or at least tolerate it long enough to get to the moments of insight.

So if I had to summarize: curiosity, persistence, honesty, a love of simplicity, and a lot of patience. And maybe also a healthy disrespect for authority, including mine.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: Well, first of all, I have been incredibly lucky with my students. Many of them went on to do remarkable things. Sepp Hochreiter, who did the LSTM with me in the 1990s. Alex Graves, who later went to DeepMind. Dan Ciresan, Ueli Meier, Jonathan Masci, Rupesh Srivastava, Klaus Greff, Faustino Gomez, and many others. So I have had a good sample to learn from.

And what I learned is this. The best ones are not necessarily the ones with the highest grades or the ones who already know the most when they arrive. The best ones share a certain stubbornness. They fall in love with a problem and they refuse to let go of it, even when everybody around them says it is hopeless or not fashionable. When Sepp and I were working on recurrent networks in the early nineties, almost nobody cared about neural networks. The field had moved on to other things. A less stubborn student would have switched topics. He did not.

The second thing is curiosity in the true sense. The good researcher is like a little scientist from childhood who never lost the urge to find out how things work, and who gets a genuine kick out of discovering a regularity that was previously unknown. This is also, by the way, the foundation of my work on artificial curiosity: the intrinsic reward comes from compression progress, from learning something that makes the world more predictable. The good student has exactly this drive built in. You cannot really teach it. You can only avoid destroying it.

Third, and this surprised me early on, the best ones are not afraid to be wrong in front of me. They come into my office and say, "I think this standard assumption is nonsense," and sometimes they are right and sometimes they are not, but the willingness to challenge is essential. The ones who only want to please the professor usually produce incremental work.

And finally, they are honest about what they do not understand. Many clever people try to hide their confusion. The really good researcher says, "I do not understand why this works," and then spends months finding out. Half of the interesting results in our lab started with somebody admitting confusion about something everyone else took for granted.

So what I learned, if I am honest, is mostly about humility. My job as an advisor was less about telling them what to do and more about protecting their time, giving them hard problems, and getting out of the way.

astra-6.text:
One thing you learn as an advisor is that the best students don’t just solve the problems you give them. They start asking questions you hadn’t thought to ask. And sometimes they convince you that your original question wasn’t the most interesting one.

That takes independence. You need enough confidence to pursue an idea when other people don’t see its value yet, but also enough humility to abandon it when the evidence goes against it. You want to be stubborn about understanding the problem, rather than stubborn about your favorite solution.

And curiosity matters enormously. If you really want to know why something works, or why it fails, then the work itself becomes rewarding. That helps you keep going through all the unsuccessful attempts. A good advisor should give that curiosity room to develop.

sol-6.1.text:
One thing I’ve learned is that you should give students room to surprise you. A really good student may take a problem in a direction that you didn’t anticipate, and then your job is to recognize that there is something interesting there, rather than insist on your original plan.

You need curiosity, of course, but also persistence and the willingness to question your own ideas. Can you turn a vague intuition into a precise question? Can you design an experiment whose result might tell you that you are wrong? And when something unexpected happens, do you investigate it? That combination of independence and intellectual honesty is very valuable.
